teaching.causalExplanation: FITT is four decisions. Frequency: how often, and so how much recovery falls between sessions. Intensity: how hard, which decides the energy system trained. Time: how long, including the work and rest inside the session. And type: which method. Here's the test for any program. Could a stranger run Monday's session from what's written? "Go hard" fails, because it isn't a number. "Build up" fails, because it isn't a plan. "Run four times a week" survives, because it's a frequency and a type a stranger could act on. Every question you'd have to ask is a decision the program didn't make. Intensity matters most, so it has to be a number. There are three ways. First, a percentage of maximum heart rate, estimated as two hundred and twenty minus age. For a sixteen-year-old, that's two hundred and four. Seventy to eighty-five per cent gives a target zone of about one hundred and forty-three to one hundred and seventy-three beats per minute. But the formula is a population average. A real sixteen-year-old's maximum can be ten or more beats either side, so treat the zone as a starting point. Second, for weights, a percentage of the heaviest load you can lift once. Third, perceived exertion, a score out of ten. It needs no equipment, so for a school squad with no monitors, it's the right choice, though beginners rate effort less accurately. The four letters look like a list, but they're linked. Intensity trades against time: the harder the effort, the shorter you can hold it, exactly like the energy systems. Intensity trades against frequency, through recovery. You adapt during recovery, not during the session, so hard work every day doesn't add fitness. It piles up fatigue. And type limits the rest. A plyometric session is short and intense by its nature. And time includes the rest: forty minutes with eight minutes of work is a different session from forty minutes of running. So within one session, if you raise one dial a lot, name the one you lower to pay for it. A program where every dial goes up at once isn't ambitious. It's unplanned.

scenes.teachingReason: Intensity matters most, so it has to be a number. There are three ways. First, a percentage of maximum heart rate, estimated as two hundred and twenty minus age. For a sixteen-year-old, that's two hundred and four. Seventy to eighty-five per cent gives a target zone of about one hundred and forty-three to one hundred and seventy-three beats per minute. But the formula is a population average. A real sixteen-year-old's maximum can be ten or more beats either side, so treat the zone as a starting point. Second, for weights, a percentage of the heaviest load you can lift once. Third, perceived exertion, a score out of ten. It needs no equipment, so for a school squad with no monitors, it's the right choice, though beginners rate effort less accurately.

scenes.teachingReason: The four letters look like a list, but they're linked. Intensity trades against time: the harder the effort, the shorter you can hold it, exactly like the energy systems. Intensity trades against frequency, through recovery. You adapt during recovery, not during the session, so hard work every day doesn't add fitness. It piles up fatigue. And type limits the rest. A plyometric session is short and intense by its nature. And time includes the rest: forty minutes with eight minutes of work is a different session from forty minutes of running. So within one session, if you raise one dial a lot, name the one you lower to pay for it. A program where every dial goes up at once isn't ambitious. It's unplanned.

scenes.teachingReason: Now "build up over the term". Once the body adapts, the same load stops being a challenge, so the program has to plan progressive overload. The safe rule is one variable at a time, in small steps. Change two at once, and if something goes wrong, you can't tell which change caused it. And plan a week where the load comes down. That's when the fatigue clears and the fitness you've built actually shows. A program that only ever goes up has confused the training with the adaptation.

scenes.teachingReason: But a program can fill in all four letters and still be wrong. FITT doesn't check that the type suits the sport. A netballer given perfect continuous running has a complete program aimed at the wrong quality. That's called specificity: training the quality the event needs. And it doesn't say what happens after six weeks, when fitness fades if training stops. Year 12 adds the principles that cover these.

scenes.teachingReason: Here's the method, on a sixteen-year-old netballer who fades in the fourth quarter. Start with the demands, not the program. Her efforts last a few seconds, but fading late is a failure to recover between them, and recovery is the aerobic system's job. So choose an aerobic program, even though her efforts are anaerobic. Time: thirty minutes, one session with four four-minute blocks at the top of the zone. Type: fartlek, because its changes of pace are closer to the game. Every number comes with its reason.
